study.title: Psalm 107 The goodness of the LORD in deliverance, provision and government
study.overview: Psalm 107 calls on the people rescued to thank the Lord for his permanent goodness and shows, in successive paintings, how God frees people in very different situations: travelers lost in the desert, prisoners in darkness, sick slaughtered, endangered navigators and communities affected by changes in the land and social life. The psalm culminates in the affirmation that God's providence must be observed wisely, so that it may be disproportionately his loyal goodness in all areas of life.

outline.title: Invitation to the praise and deliverance of the erring
outline.explanation: The psalm begins with a call for them to be redeemed by the LORD. He then describes lost and hungry people in the desert, without city to live, who cry out to God and are guided to the right path, receiving provision and motive for public gratitude.

outline.title: Deliverment of rebels, prisoners and sick
outline.explanation: The second part presents those who suffered in darkness and imprisonment for having rebelled against the commandments of God, besides the fools afflicted by their transgressions. In all cases, the cry to the Lord is answered with deliverance, healing and restoration, demanding thanksgiving and proclamation of divine works.

outline.title: The Lord on the sea and the assembly of the people
outline.explanation: Here appear those who go down to the sea and see the works of the Lord in the depths. God raises the storm, calms the waves and leads travelers to the desired port. The text then extends the correct answer: public praise in the assembly and at the meeting of the elders.

outline.title: God's rule on earth and the call to wisdom
outline.explanation: The final part shows that the LORD also transforms rivers into a desert and desert into a pond, demolishing or raising peoples according to their providence. The righteous rejoice to see this, and the wise man is called to reflect on these things and to perceive the goodness of the Lord.

study.context: According to the notes provided, the psalm is a hymn of praise to the God the Redeemer, possibly linked to those who returned from exile, although this is not affirmed with certainty by the biblical text itself. Matthew Henry's commentary emphasizes that the psalm deals with God's providence of humanity in general, not just about Israel, while Tyndale and Adam Clarke observe that he brings together four examples of deliverance and then concludes with a call to the wise observation of divine providence.
study.theology: The psalm teaches that the goodness of the Lord is constant and that his mercy does not fail. The repetition of the cry and the divine response shows that deliverance does not come from human force, but from God's graceful intervention. The text also links suffering and sin in some cases, without reducing all suffering to personal guilt; in others, it shows that danger can come simply from the fragile condition of life. Thus, God's providence encompasses desert, imprisonment, sickness, revolting sea, land fertility and social relations. The conclusion calls for discernment: the wise not only receives benefits, but interprets history as an expression of God's faithful goodness. The commentator notes also highlight that justice remains in the work of God and that his loyal goodness is the main mark of his performance.

scholarViews.insight: The psalm ends with an invitation to discern God's infallible love in all areas of life.
The rescued have a special reason to say that God is good and that his mercy endures forever.
The wise man is called to observe, keep in the heart and reflect on these things to understand the constant goodness of the Lord.

questions: In what situations of your life have you acted as someone who needs to cry out to the Lord instead of relying on only own resources?
Do you recognize the goodness of God only when you receive deliverance, or when He corrects, leads and governs difficult circumstances?
How can your community turn gratitude into public praise and a testimony of God's works?
study.practice: Read the psalm remembering that it describes not only one kind of distress, but various forms of human need. Then identify a concrete area in which you need direction, healing, provision or liberation, and present it to God in simple and confident prayer. Then practice specific gratitude: name at least three signs of the Lord's goodness in your recent history and share one of them with someone else to glorify God publicly.
study.uncertainty: The notes provided suggest, but do not demonstrate conclusively, a connection with exile; therefore this context should be treated as an interpretative possibility, not as a certain fact. It is also not possible to safely state whether each p.m. frame describes a specific historical group or a broader picture of human experience, because the text itself and notes allow more general reading.
